response.answer: Under the updated rule (89 FR 106064, Doc. 2024-29957), a food must generally meet two main criteria to use the 'healthy' implied nutrient content claim: (1) it must contain a specified amount of a food group equivalent (FGE) from at least one food group encouraged by the Dietary Guidelines, 2020–2025 (vegetables, fruits, whole grains, fat-free or low-fat dairy, lean meat, seafood, eggs, beans, peas, lentils, nuts, or seeds), and (2) it must not exceed specified nutrient-to-limit (NTL) thresholds for added sugars, saturated fat, and sodium, based on a percentage of the Daily Value for those nutrients. These two criteria—food group equivalent requirements and limits on nutrients to limit—are described in 21 CFR 101.65(d)(3)(ii) through (v) and summarized in the preamble at 89 FR 106064. As stated in the background section of 90 FR 10592 (Doc. 2025-03118): the rule 'requires that, to bear a claim subject to the rule, individual food products, mixed products, main dishes, and meals must meet FGEs and specific limits for added sugars, saturated fat, and sodium based on a percentage of the Daily Value for these nutrients.' Certain categories of foods (e.g., those composed solely of encouraged food groups with no added ingredients other than water, and water/tea/coffee with less than 5 calories) automatically qualify without meeting both criteria, per 21 CFR 101.65(d)(3)(i) and (vi).

The 'healthy' implied nutrient content claim is governed by 21 CFR 101.65(d). This section, titled 'Implied nutrient content claims and related label statements,' contains paragraph (d) ('General nutritional claims') which specifically defines the conditions under which the term 'healthy' or related derivative terms may be used as an implied nutrient content claim on food labeling (21 CFR 101.65(d)(2)–(3)). The general definition of an implied nutrient content claim, including the 'healthy' example, is also set forth in 21 CFR 101.13(b)(2)(ii), which states that an implied nutrient content claim includes any claim that 'suggests that a food, because of its nutrient content, may be useful in maintaining healthy dietary practices, where there is also implied or explicit information about the nutrition content of the food (e.g., "healthy")' (21 CFR 101.13(b)(2)(ii)). The final rule updating the definition of 'healthy' was published at 89 FR 106064 (Doc. 2024-29957), with an effective date of April 28, 2025 (as revised by Doc. 2025-03118) and a compliance date of February 25, 2028.

Your compliance date is February 25, 2028. The final rule (Doc. 2024-29957, 89 FR 106064, published 2024-12-27) states a single compliance date of February 25, 2028 for all regulated parties subject to the updated 'healthy' nutrient content claim requirements under 21 CFR 101.65(d). FDA explicitly considered and rejected a request to provide small businesses with an additional 2 years beyond the general compliance date (see Response 135 in the preamble, 89 FR 106064). The agency stated it did not have sufficient information to justify a different compliance timeline for small businesses and was concerned about consumer confusion from having different versions of the 'healthy' claim in the market for a longer period. Therefore, no size-based or revenue-based extended compliance date exists in this rule. Note that while the effective date was delayed from February 25, 2025 to April 28, 2025 by Doc. 2025-03118 (90 FR 10592), that document explicitly states 'the compliance date remains unchanged at this time.' Your $8M in annual food sales does not entitle you to any additional time.

response.answer:
No, that was not a fair reading in mid-2025, and it is definitively incorrect now.

**What was true in mid-2025:** The January 2025 order revoking FD&C Red No. 3 (90 FR 4628, published 2025-01-16, Doc. 2025-00830) was subject to an automatic administrative stay under 21 U.S.C. 371(e)(2) as of February 18, 2025, triggered by the filing of objections. During that stay, the effective dates of January 15, 2027 (food uses, removal of 21 CFR 74.303) and January 18, 2028 (ingested drugs, removal of 21 CFR 74.1303) were suspended pending FDA's resolution of the objections. However, the order itself was a final binding order — not a proposal — and the stay was a procedural pause, not a substantive reversal. The stay did not change the stated effective dates; it merely suspended their operation temporarily. Saying the removal was 'not final and might never take effect' overstated the situation: the order was final, and the stay would end either by FDA overruling the objections or by FDA modifying/revoking the order. The Delaney Clause finding (that FD&C Red No. 3 causes cancer in laboratory animals) left FDA essentially no discretion to reverse the revocation on the merits (90 FR 4628 at section VI, Doc. 2025-00830).

**What is the position now:** FDA published a final action on August 5, 2026 (91 FR 50475, Doc. 2026-15920) overruling all objections, denying requests for a public hearing, and lifting the administrative stay. The document explicitly confirms the original effective dates: January 15, 2027 for the repeal of § 74.303 (food) and January 18, 2028 for the repeal of § 74.1303 (ingested drugs). This constitutes 'final action on the objections' under section 701(e)(2) of the FD&C Act. The revocation is fully confirmed and binding.

Because no compliance date was separately stated in the January 2025 order, the operative deadlines are derived from the effective dates: food products containing FD&C Red No. 3 will be adulterated as of January 15, 2027, and ingested drugs containing it will be adulterated as of January 18, 2028 (Doc. 2025-00830, section VI; Doc. 2026-15920, section V).

response.answer:
The order published at 90 FR 4628 (Doc. 2025-00830, published January 16, 2025) changes three CFR provisions within 21 CFR Part 74, and they do NOT all change on the same day. The amendatory instructions are:

1. **Amendatory Instruction 2 – Remove 21 CFR 74.303** (FD&C Red No. 3 for food use). This removes the entire listing that authorizes FD&C Red No. 3 as a color additive in food (including dietary supplements). Effective date: **January 15, 2027** (90 FR 4628; confirmed by 91 FR 50475).

2. **Amendatory Instruction 3 – Revise 21 CFR 74.1303** (FD&C Red No. 3 for ingested drugs). Because § 74.1303 cross-references the identity and specifications in § 74.303(a)(1) and (b), the order revises § 74.1303 to incorporate that information directly so it can stand alone after § 74.303 is removed. Effective date: **January 15, 2027** (same as the removal of § 74.303) (90 FR 4628 at preamble section VI; 2025-00830#0000).

3. **Amendatory Instruction 4 – Remove 21 CFR 74.1303** (FD&C Red No. 3 for ingested drugs). This removes the entire listing that authorizes FD&C Red No. 3 in ingested drugs. Effective date: **January 18, 2028** (90 FR 4628; confirmed by 91 FR 50475).

Thus there are two distinct effective dates. The food-use revocation (removal of § 74.303 and the interim revision of § 74.1303) takes effect January 15, 2027, while the ingested-drug revocation (removal of § 74.1303) takes effect January 18, 2028. No separate compliance date is stated in the order; the operative deadlines are derived from the effective dates (per 2025-00830). The order was administratively stayed from February 18, 2025, through August 5, 2026, but the stay did not change any dates; both effective dates were confirmed by 91 FR 50475 (Doc. 2026-15920).

response.answer: Under 21 CFR 101.65(a)(2), a 'healthy' implied nutrient content claim must be made in accordance with the general requirements for nutrient content claims in § 101.13, with one specific carve-out: § 101.13(h) is excepted when the nutrient content claim is made in accordance with paragraph (d) of § 101.65. Section 101.13(h) is the disclosure requirement that would otherwise mandate a statement such as 'See nutrition information for ___ content' when a food exceeds specified levels of fat, saturated fat, cholesterol, or sodium. This carve-out means that a food bearing the 'healthy' claim under § 101.65(d) is not required to include the § 101.13(h) disclosure statement, even if the food would otherwise trigger it. All other general requirements of § 101.13 (e.g., type size limitations under § 101.13(f), the definition of implied claims under § 101.13(b)(2), and other provisions) still apply to a 'healthy' claim.

response.answer: Yes, your shelf-stable lentil soup labeled 'healthy' is affected by the updated definition of the term 'healthy' under the final rule published at 89 FR 106064 (Doc. 2024-29957, published 2024-12-27). This rule revises 21 CFR 101.65(d) to establish new food-group-equivalent (FGE) and nutrient-to-limit (NTL) criteria for foods bearing the 'healthy' implied nutrient content claim. Under the new framework, your lentil soup would need to qualify under one of the pathways in § 101.65(d)(3): either as a food comprised solely of qualifying ingredients with no other added ingredients except water (paragraph (d)(3)(i), which lists beans, peas, and lentils among qualifying foods), or as a mixed product meeting the FGE and NTL requirements in paragraph (d)(3)(iii), depending on its formulation. Until that compliance date, you may continue to use the 'healthy' claim under the prior criteria, but you must comply with the new requirements by February 25, 2028.
